raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.title: Two villages cleared for the Raciborz Dolny flood polder
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.place: Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska, gmina Lubomia, Silesian Voivodeship, Poland
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.point: The locality of Nieboczowy in gmina Lubomia, as OpenStreetMap records it. This is the old village site inside the dry polder basin; the replacement village was built about 7 km away near Syrynia, in the same commune.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Odra River Basin Flood Protection Project, P086768, loan IBRD-74360. Approved 21 March 2007, closed 30 June 2020 after a six-year extension. US$184 million committed and US$166.56 million disbursed, against a total project cost of US$1.019 billion; in euros the completion report gives 131.94 million disbursed of an original commitment of 140.1 million, about 91 per cent (completion report, 28 January 2021). The completion report rates the outcome Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 10 June 2021 also rates it Satisfactory.

lenders.name: European Commission
lenders.role: Co-financier through the EU Cohesion Fund. The completion report's cost-overrun table gives 340.56 million euros disbursed at closing against 130 million estimated at appraisal (completion report, 28 January 2021).

lenders.name: Council of Europe Development Bank
lenders.role: Co-financier. The completion report's cost-overrun table gives 204.66 million euros disbursed at closing against 204.9 million estimated at appraisal, and records that the Bank and the Development Bank ran joint project review missions (completion report, 28 January 2021).

companies.name: Regional Authority for Water Management in Gliwice (RZGW Gliwice)
companies.role: State water authority for the upper Odra basin, and the project implementation unit for the Raciborz dry polder and for the resettlement. It later became part of PGW WP, the State Water Holding Polish Waters. The completion report names no construction contractor.

companies.name: Lower Silesian Board for Amelioration and Hydraulic Structures (DZMiUW)
companies.role: The regional water-engineering board that carried out land acquisition for the Wroclaw floodway works, supervised alongside the new village construction (completion report, 28 January 2021).

raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.community: The Raciborz Dolny dry polder was built on the land of two villages, Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska. The completion report of 28 January 2021 says the process "included around 700 individuals belonging to about 250 households", and that "aside from the houses, church, and cemetery, all public facilities needed to be relocated". The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 10 June 2021 gives the same figures: "250 families were resettled, representing about 700 residents". A new village with all services was built for them near Syrynia, about 7 km from the old site. The appraisal document of 21 February 2007 records that the polder needed about 2,600 ha of land, that 20 businesses were in the polder area, most of which would be relocated or closed, and that 22 community assets would be closed or relocated, including a church, a chapel, seven crosses, five wayside shrines, a cemetery, two fire brigade buildings, a kindergarten, a school, a bread house, a recreation room and a sports club. Thirteen wayside shrines and conciliation crosses were moved to the new village. Most houses were bought by agreement over 2003 to 2012: the resettlement plan update of March 2015 counts about 68 buildings acquired by 2006, 1 in 2007, 14 in 2008, 11 in 2009, 8 in 2010, 16 in 2011 and 55 in 2012. In 2013, 30 houses were acquired under an administrative decision of the Silesian Voivodeship of 26 November 2012 rather than by agreement. Opposition was organised and long-running. A Committee for the Defence of Nieboczowy against Displacement was formally constituted in March 2002; the same plan update records 150 appeals against the location permit lodged with the Ministry of Infrastructure and 18 at the Administrative Court in Warsaw, with the Supreme Administrative Court rejecting the complaints on 27 April 2007. A 1998 survey of the two villages found 91.9 per cent of residents formally accepted displacement; a July 2002 survey of the same population found 42.2 per cent gave express consent and 29.4 per cent refused outright. The completion report says there was "strong initial opposition, even leading to violent resistance", and that the project then built support through consultation; it says the resettled people "have indicated repeatedly that they are content with the new situation", and the Bank presents the resettlement as international best practice. RMF24 reported in April 2007 that about 200 residents were blocking the reservoir and would leave only if the whole village, including the church, was moved with them. The Catholic weekly Gosc Niedzielny reported on 30 June 2020, when the reservoir opened, that Nieboczowy's residents had jointly asked to be relocated and that the new village was built from scratch about 7 km away.
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.displaced_label: people resettled from Nieboczowy and Ligota Tworkowska, about 250 households, per the World Bank completion report of 28 January 2021 and the Independent Evaluation Group review of 10 June 2021
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 689 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The project documents give about 700 residents in about 250 households for the two villages. The documents do not explain the difference between the two figures.
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.killed_note: No death caused by the project or its contractors is recorded in the completion report.
raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.outcome: The polder was made operational in January 2020 and the reservoir was formally opened on 30 June 2020. The old village sites are inside the polder basin. The replacement village of Nieboczowy near Syrynia is built and occupied. Both the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group rate the project's outcome Satisfactory.

raciborz-polder-nieboczowy-village-remov.confidence_note: The counts of people and households moved, the village demolition and the 2013 acquisition of 30 houses by administrative decision all come from the lender's own documents and its borrower's resettlement plan. Polish press independent of the lender confirms that the village stood where the polder embankments now are, that it was rebuilt about 7 km away, and that about 200 residents were blocking the project in 2007. The press accounts and the Bank's documents differ in emphasis: one 2020 report says residents jointly asked to be relocated, while the lender's own completion report records initial opposition that reached violent resistance. No document gives a count of people compelled to move against their will; the 30 houses taken by administrative decision in 2013 is the only compulsion figure in the documents.

hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.title: Shala neighbourhood cleared for lignite mining, and years in temporary housing
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.place: Shala neighbourhood of Hade village, Obiliq municipality, Kosovo
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.point: Hade village, Obiliq municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. The Shala neighbourhood was part of Hade. The resettlement site, Shkabaj or New Hade, is about 8 km east, nearer Pristina.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Energy Sector Clean-up and Land Reclamation Project, P096181, grants IDA-H2340 and IDA-H3190 and credit IDA-52400, with trust funds TF-13509 and TF-90160. Approved 13 June 2006, closed 31 August 2016. The second additional financing, approved 10 May 2013 and filed separately as P131539, added US$4.2 million and created Component F, which paid for monitoring of the Resettlement Action Plan for the Shala neighbourhood. The completion report of 28 February 2017 rates the outcome Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 29 June 2017. The completion report states that the project "did not cause nor finance the resettlement; it only supervised MESP's responsibility to implement the RAP". The Resettlement Action Plan itself was a technical assistance output of another Bank-financed project, the Lignite Power Technical Assistance Project, in 2011.

lenders.name: Netherlands Ministry for Development Cooperation
lenders.role: Co-financier. A grant of US$4.33 million agreed in December 2006 covered the original project's financing gap, and a second grant of US$1.2 million came with the second additional financing (completion report, 28 February 2017).

companies.name: Korporata Energjetike e Kosoves (KEK)
companies.role: Kosovo's energy corporation, which the completion report's abbreviation list writes as "Kosovo Energy Cooperation". It operates the Kosovo A and Kosovo B lignite power plants and the mines that supply them; the project was designed in part to build capacity inside it for clean-up and mining operations. Its mine expansion took the land of the Shala neighbourhood, and it paid the compensation and the temporary rent allowances.

companies.name: Ministry of Environment and Spatial Planning of Kosovo (MESP)
companies.role: The ministry responsible for implementing the Shala Resettlement Action Plan, including building the water, sewage and electricity infrastructure at the resettlement site. It ran the grievance commission, which the resettlement completion report says stopped working.

companies.name: rePlan Inc.
companies.role: The international resettlement consultancy commissioned to prepare the Shala Resettlement Action Plan and then, under the Bank-financed Component F, to monitor and report on its implementation.

hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.community: KEK's lignite mine expansion took the Shala neighbourhood of Hade village. The resettlement completion report of July 2016 counts 93 affected households: 63 of them, with 320 full-time residents, were resident households that "needed to be physically displaced", and the other 30 lost land only. By June 2015 the report records 0 of the 63 households still living in Shala. In January 2012, 21 of the 93 households were found to be in a risk zone, were required to leave at once, and were given a monthly rent and living allowance. The Inspection Panel, which visited in 2015, records residents saying they had been in temporary housing since 2011 or 2012 and only received their plots in late 2014. Rent and food assistance was stopped in April 2014; the Panel report says the site was still not ready and many households were still in rented housing. The Bank's completion report says the resettlement was in breach of the Resettlement Action Plan and of the project's legal covenants by December 2013, and that the Bank threatened to suspend disbursements; the breach was resolved when KEK approved more rent payments for the 21 families. The report also records untimely payment of the temporary rent allowances as putting the project in bad standing with its legal covenants. Rebuilding was slow. The resettlement completion report counts 52 of 52 plots allocated with title deeds issued by June 2015, 48 construction permits issued, 22 plots with construction started or finished, 15 houses ready to live in and 12 occupied, with 53 people living at the new site. Three houses that were ready stood empty in February 2016 because the sewage collecting pipe was blocked. Residents reported 50 metres of blocked sewage pipe in October 2015 and the ministry estimated that about 200 metres needed replacing. Three of the 30 households that lost land only had still not claimed their compensation in February 2016. In the 2015 survey of 32 households, 43.8 per cent said their economic situation was worse than a year before, against 23.1 per cent in 2011; among the households that lost land without moving, 62.5 per cent said they were worse off. The same report concludes that "livelihoods and living conditions have been at least restored and in some instances improved", and that compensation complied with the Bank's resettlement policy. Residents told the Inspection Panel a different story: that compensation was set on a 2004 valuation, that they had to pay the difference between the value of their old plots and the new ones, which they put at about 12,500 euros, that their new plots were smaller, that 20 jobs KEK was to provide under a 2011 agreement had not all materialised, that there was no school or clinic near the site, and that they had never been told of any grievance mechanism.
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.displaced_label: households physically displaced from the Shala neighbourhood, holding 320 full-time residents, per the resettlement completion report of July 2016; the same report records 0 of the 63 still living in Shala as of June 2015
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 407 for this project, which is its count of project-affected people and not a count of people moved. The project documents count 93 affected households, of which 63 with 320 full-time residents were physically displaced.
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents or the Inspection Panel report.
hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.outcome: The Shala neighbourhood is gone and the mine has expanded over it. The Inspection Panel investigated and its report went to the Bank's board in 2016. The Bank's management agreed to three follow-up actions: repairing a 200-metre section of clogged sewage, technical assistance to revise the resettlement policy framework, and a workshop with the government and KEK. The completion report says the sewage was repaired by December 2016 and the workshop was held on 14 February 2017, and notes that only the sewage repair is directly linked to the project. At the project's closing in August 2016, 12 of the 52 households that chose a plot at the new site were living there. In September 2016 KEK opened negotiations with several hundred more residents who are to be moved for new excavations.

hade-shala-neighbourhood-mine-resettleme.confidence_note: The counts rest on the resettlement completion report that the lender paid for, but the Inspection Panel visited the site, took evidence from residents and published its own account, and Kosovo press and CEE Bankwatch reported on the Panel's investigation. Two accounts of what the Panel found do not agree. The Independent Evaluation Group's review says the Panel found the Bank's approach and supervision in compliance with the resettlement policy, with "two minor instances of non-compliance" over asset valuation, infrastructure delays and malfunctioning sewage. Prishtina Insight, which saw the leaked investigation report, says the Panel found that the Bank's management did not comply with its resettlement procedures, that the resettlement policy framework lacked methods for valuing the assets of people under the mining-field restrictions, and that the Bank's failings contributed to "real and often severe harm" over a prolonged period. The Panel's 2016 investigation report itself could not be opened; both accounts are given here. The lender states that the project did not cause or finance the resettlement and only monitored it, while the resettlement plan it rests on was prepared under a different Bank-financed project.

tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.title: Motorway built on land whose owners had not been paid
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.place: Tabanovce to Kumanovo, Corridor X, North Macedonia
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.point: Tabanovce, Kumanovo municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. The upgraded section runs 7.3 km from the Tabanovce border crossing to Kumanovo.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Second Trade and Transport Facilitation Project, P091723, loan IBRD-48590. Approved 29 May 2007, closed 30 June 2012 after a nine-month extension. Loan of 15 million euros, equivalent to US$20 million; US$20.52 million disbursed. In March 2009 the Bank sent a Warning of Suspension of Disbursement for the part of the loan covering the road upgrade. The completion report of 12 December 2012 rates the outcome Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 12 September 2013.

companies.name: Agency for State Roads
companies.role: The national road agency and the implementing body for the road upgrade, including land acquisition and compensation payments; its Director was the project coordinator. The revised resettlement plan required it to hold the full assessed compensation in a special account. The completion report names no construction contractor, referring only to "the contractor".

companies.name: Customs Administration
companies.role: A unit of the Ministry of Finance, and the implementing body for the Blace border crossing component, where 27 parcels of land had to be acquired that the government had told the Bank would not be needed.

tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.community: Land was taken for the 7.3 km upgrade of the Tabanovce to Kumanovo section of Corridor X to motorway standard. The completion report of 12 December 2012 records "about 102 affected owners involving about 294 parcels of land". In March 2009 the Bank's team found that compensation for that land "was not paid to all landowners prior to start of works by the contractor", contrary to the Resettlement Action Plan and the loan agreement, because some owners had gone to court to raise the amounts. The report calls the delays in payment "a serious safeguard violation". The Bank sent a Warning of Suspension of Disbursement for the road part of the loan. The warning was lifted a few months later when the Bank and the government agreed to amend the plan and the loan agreement so that works could proceed as long as money for compensation was set aside in the road agency's budget; the national law was changed in the same direction. Four or five court cases were still open when the project closed; the report says they have since been decided, and that under Macedonian law payment from the state budget follows automatically once a court makes an award. At the Blace crossing to Kosovo, the government assured the Bank during preparation that no land acquisition was needed; at implementation 27 parcels had to be acquired, and the completion report says this held up the start of civil works for more than two years. No resettlement of people and no demolition of permanent structures took place.
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 294 for this project. The completion report's figure of about 294 is a count of land parcels, not of people: the same sentence gives about 102 affected owners. No project document records anyone being relocated.
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents.
tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.outcome: The motorway is open and the completion report says all land acquisition cases have been resolved. The safeguard violation is recorded in both the completion report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review; the review says it was "quickly" addressed. No independent record of how much the owners who went to court were finally paid was found.

tabanovce-kumanovo-motorway-compensation.confidence_note: The harm is squarely stated in the lender's own completion report and repeated in its evaluation arm's review, which is as strong as a lender record gets. It is still a lender reporting on its own project: no court record, audit or news report about the affected owners was found, and the documents give no figure for how much any owner was eventually paid, nor how long any owner waited.

igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.title: A road worker killed and a resident's house damaged on the Igoeti highway works
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.place: Igoeti village, Kaspi municipality, Shida Kartli, Georgia
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.point: Igoeti village, Kaspi municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. The project upgraded the 24 km of the E60 highway from Igoeti to Sveneti and built the Igoeti bypass and its four bridges.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Second East-West Highway Improvement Project, P094044, credits IDA-43730 and IDA-45120. Approved 18 December 2007, closed 30 June 2012. XDR 34.72 million disbursed. The completion report of 28 December 2012 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 28 October 2013.

companies.name: Roads Department of Georgia
companies.role: The national road agency, moved in the 2009 ministerial reforms from the Ministry of Economic Development to the new Ministry of Regional Development and Infrastructure, and the project's implementing agency. Its Resettlement Unit, four staff plus a hired consultant, handled land acquisition and compensation. The completion report does not name the construction contractors, calling them "the first road contractor" and the contractor hired in June 2011.

igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.community: One of the first road contractor's local employees was killed while performing a pavement test on the project section. The completion report of 28 December 2012 says he was "killed by a speeding car whose driver ignored a road construction warning sign", and that the contractor "refused to pay compensation to the victim's family for about 1.5 years, despite constant reminders by the Bank Team" and the Roads Department. The report's lessons section says the accident shows that traffic safety during road construction works remains a problem, and that payment to a contractor should be refused where it has not met safety requirements. The same contractor started civil works before land acquisition from a resident of Igoeti village was officially completed, and in doing so damaged her house and made improper use of her land. That case stayed open from 2009 until 25 June 2012, when she signed an agreement accepting GEL 11,139, about US$6,700, for 954 square metres of land and 62 fruit trees; payment took effect on 9 July 2012. She had already been paid GEL 45,000, about US$27,270, in February 2011 for damage to her summer house during construction. The report says the first contractor's work was unsatisfactory in many instances, that it knew of design errors and "took advantage of the situation", and that it failed to comply with the environmental management plan, especially on storage and disposal of materials. Land take ran well beyond the original plan: the number of plots in the right of way reached 192, covering 146,914 square metres, against the resettlement plan's own figure, and about 4 more hectares of private land were needed for connecting roads to neighbouring villages. The completion report says all compensation was paid by the end of the project, totalling GEL 1,343,773, about US$0.81 million, and that all outstanding cases were resolved to the satisfaction of the affected people.
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.killed_note: One local employee of the road contractor was killed on the project section while performing a pavement test. The completion report attributes the death to a speeding driver who ignored a road construction warning sign, so it is not counted here; the report's own lesson is that traffic safety on construction sites should be enforced by the employer and the supervision consultants.
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 607 for this project. No project document records anyone being relocated: the appraisal document said no physical relocation was expected, and the completion report records land and tree compensation only.
igoeti-sveneti-highway-worker-death-and-.outcome: The highway section is built. The first contractor's contract was allowed to expire and another contractor was hired in June 2011 to finish the works and repair the defective ones. The family of the dead worker was paid after about a year and a half, according to the completion report, which does not give the amount. The Igoeti land case closed with payment in July 2012.

ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.title: Farm land taken for drainage works before the resettlement plan covered it
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.place: Bagdad, Rishtan and Altiaryk districts, Fergana region, Uzbekistan
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.point: Bagdad (Bog'dod) town, Bagdad district, Fergana region, as OpenStreetMap records it. Bagdad is one of the three districts where land was taken; the project area covers about 67,000 ha across the three.

lenders.name: World Bank (IDA)
lenders.role: Ferghana Valley Water Resources Management Project Phase I, P110538, credit IDA-46480. Approved 24 September 2009, closed 31 December 2016. XDR 33.76 million disbursed. The safeguards compliance rating was downgraded during implementation over the land acquisition and later upgraded. The completion report of 16 May 2017 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 16 October 2017.

companies.name: Projects Implementation Unit for Water Infrastructure, Ministry of Agriculture and Water Resources of Uzbekistan
companies.role: The unit inside the national water ministry that ran the project, prepared the resettlement plans and the land acquisition reports, and operated the grievance mechanism. Compensation amounts were set by decisions of the Fergana regional governor (khakim) and the district governors.

ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.community: Rehabilitating drainage and irrigation canals took farm land, permanently and temporarily, and removed trees along roads, canals and drains. The resettlement plan prepared before appraisal and updated in 2011 covered 37 farmers. The completion report of 16 May 2017 says that "between 2012 and 2014, 338 farmers were affected by the project activities, and land acquisition took place without the RAP being updated, which constituted a noncompliance with the World Bank OP 4.12", because local authorities would not approve updates until the list of farmers was final. The report also says that "compensation payments were done with delay after land acquisition and/or civil works started", blaming invalid bank details and suspended bank accounts, and that "in most cases, the PAPs did not receive any cash as compensation was used to settle outstanding tax arrears". It adds that some farmers who were paid turned out not to be affected at all, and that there was no mechanism to recover those payments. The borrower's own report on land acquisition in 2012 to 2014, dated November 2015, puts figures to it. Under four decisions of the Fergana regional governor between October 2011 and April 2014, 513 farm enterprises were due compensation and 373 were paid, UZS 937,803,509 in total, leaving UZS 980,473,630 to be paid by the end of 2015. Of 189 land users covered by the December 2013 decision, 155 were paid; of 128 under the February 2014 decision, 60 were paid; of 159 under the April 2014 decision, 123 were paid. A further decision of 25 December 2014 assessed damage of UZS 494,989,548, and the report says no payment had been made under it because funds had to be reallocated. The report explains some gaps: in 2012, 10 of 34 unpaid farm enterprises had no damage because part of the collector works was dropped at detailed design, while money for the remaining 24 came back because bank account details were wrong. Land taken by year ran 515.25 ha in 2012, 334.51 ha in 2013, 334.52 ha and a further 226.57 ha in 2014 and 197.49 ha in 2015. The completion report says all outstanding payments were made before the project closed, and that the use of compensation against tax arrears "did not seem to cause any unhappiness in the farmers' community".
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 263 for this project. No project document records anyone being relocated; the figures in the documents count farmers and farm enterprises whose land was taken, not people moved.
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents.
ferghana-valley-drainage-land-taken-with.outcome: The drainage works were built and the project closed in December 2016 with the outstanding compensation paid, according to the completion report. The two evaluation documents do not agree about compliance: the completion report of 2017 calls the land acquisition without an updated plan a non-compliance with the Bank's resettlement policy, while the Independent Evaluation Group's field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 29 March 2019 says "overall, the project complied with the implementation of safeguards" and that "previous reviews of the safeguards confirmed full compliance".

yenice-logistic-village-urgent-expropria.title: Urgent expropriation at Yenice for a railway logistics village
yenice-logistic-village-urgent-expropria.place: Yenice, Tarsus district, Mersin province, Turkey
yenice-logistic-village-urgent-expropria.point: Yenice village, Tarsus district, Mersin, as OpenStreetMap records it. Yenice sits at the railway junction where the logistics village and the expropriated parcels are.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Railways Restructuring Project, P077328, loan IBRD-47870. US$184.70 million committed, US$148.05 million disbursed. The project was restructured in 2011 to deal with land acquisition and building works that triggered the Bank's involuntary resettlement policy, which had not been triggered at appraisal; the Bank then required the state railway to prepare a Resettlement Action Plan covering the project-affected people, particularly at the Yenice logistics village, and created loan obligations to implement it. The completion report of 3 December 2015 rates the outcome Moderately Unsatisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 30 June 2016, which also rates Bank performance Moderately Unsatisfactory.

companies.name: Turkiye Cumhuriyeti Devlet Demiryollari (TCDD)
companies.role: The Turkish state railway company, which owns and runs the national network and was the project's implementing agency. Its executive board decided on 25 January 2008 to move road-haulage and loading operations out of the Adana train terminal and to expropriate land at the Yenice terminal for a logistics village; its regional directorates carried out the expropriation.

yenice-logistic-village-urgent-expropria.community: The project's resettlement plan of March 2011 records that at Yenice the method chosen was "urgent expropriation" under Article 27 of Turkey's Expropriation Law, authorised by a Council of Ministers decree of 31 March 2008, in order to speed up the project. Under that article the administration may seize the property first and settle everything but the valuation later. The first and second courts of first instance in Tarsus set the expropriation value of 155 parcels at TRY 17,977,032.97. TCDD then narrowed the area to 277,249.71 square metres and valued 47 parcels belonging to private owners, covering 220,553.71 square metres, at TRY 5,620,188.46. At a settlement meeting on 16 to 18 June 2010, four parcel owners accepted the valuation and transferred title. On 30 June 2010 TCDD paid TRY 5,308,128.58, the value the Tarsus courts had set, into accounts opened in the parcel owners' names, and the courts granted TCDD permission to enter the land. For the 43 parcels where no agreement was reached, valuation and registration lawsuits were filed on 14 July 2010; by the date of the plan the court's experts had visited 16 of those sites. The plan's socio-economic survey, carried out between May and July 2010, interviewed 42 households holding 181 people. It records that "at the time of the survey in June 2010 no resettlement was anticipated. However, land expropriation has been carried out since then." For the project's own works the plan set out 74 parcels totalling 302,388.16 square metres to be bought at an estimated TRY 9.2 million, with 41 households losing land, 15 households whose farm income would fall, three poultry farms affected and three households whose houses would be affected. It put the loss of income for owners at between 1.6 and 74 per cent, with two households losing more than 45 per cent. No completion document counts the land finally taken, the households finally paid, or how the 43 court cases ended.
yenice-logistic-village-urgent-expropria.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 256 for this project. No project document records anyone being relocated. The plan's socio-economic survey counted 181 people in 42 households whose land was affected, and three households whose houses were affected.
yenice-logistic-village-urgent-expropria.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents.
yenice-logistic-village-urgent-expropria.outcome: The completion report of 3 December 2015 says only that the need for land acquisition arose at the passing loops and near the Yenice logistics village, that this was handled in the second restructuring, and that later safeguard reviews raised "fairly minor issues". The Independent Evaluation Group's review adds that the land acquisition arose from activities "not financed by the project but adjacent to the project". Neither document gives any count of land acquired or compensation paid, and no Turkish court record or news report of the Yenice expropriations was found.

yenice-logistic-village-urgent-expropria.confidence_note: The expropriation record comes from one document, the borrower's resettlement plan of March 2011, which is the only document in the set that reports what happened at Yenice. It is a plan, but the Yenice section is written in the past tense and names decrees, court decisions and dates. The link to the lender needs stating plainly: the logistics village was not financed by the loan, and the lender's own review calls it adjacent to the project rather than part of it. The lender nevertheless brought it inside the project's resettlement plan and created loan obligations to implement that plan. How the 43 unresolved court cases ended is not recorded in any document found.

dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.title: Compensation paid two years late at Dartlo, and grievances left two years at Telavi
dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.place: Dartlo village, Tusheti, Akhmeta municipality, Kakheti, Georgia
dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.point: Dartlo village, Akhmeta municipality, as OpenStreetMap records it. Dartlo is one of three sub-project sites where resettlement impacts occurred; the other two are the towns of Telavi and Kvareli, about 70 and 90 km to the south.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Regional Development Project, P126033, loan IBRD-81480. Approved 20 March 2012, closed 31 December 2017. US$60 million committed, US$57.27 million disbursed, of a total project cost of US$72.18 million. The completion report of 18 June 2018 rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory and Bank performance Satisfactory; the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 21 September 2018 also rates the outcome Moderately Satisfactory.

companies.name: Municipal Development Fund of Georgia (MDF)
companies.role: The state fund that finances and manages municipal investment works and was the project's implementing agency, with the Ministry of Finance as borrower. It prepared and implemented the abbreviated resettlement plans and ran the grievance mechanism; its safeguards staff grew from 5 to 12 during the project.

companies.name: National Agency for Cultural Heritage Preservation of Georgia
companies.role: The state heritage agency, which cleared designs and developed the second phase sub-project for Dartlo, a protected heritage village (completion report, 18 June 2018).

dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.community: Three sub-projects moved people or interrupted their livelihoods: Dartlo, a protected village high in Tusheti, and the towns of Telavi and Kvareli. The completion report of 18 June 2018 says the Kvareli plan covered temporary income losses of 33 people, the Telavi plan covered temporary relocation and business interruption for 91 households and 84 businesses, and the Dartlo plan covered 44 residential buildings whose owners had to move out for the duration of the works. The resettlement plan update for Dartlo, dated July 2016, records what happened in the first season. Works started on 33 buildings in 2012, all of them in the category whose residents were required to relocate temporarily. "In 2012, no one owner of the buildings has received the compensations." Of the owners entitled, compensation due for 2012 to 21 affected persons was paid in 2014 to 19 of them, and two were still waiting, with payment planned for 2016 once the plan was updated. The update also records that in 2012 none of the buildings was officially registered and owners were identified from villagers' verbal statements, which later changed who was entitled: one building recorded as having a single owner turned out to have three. At Telavi, the completion report says 37 grievances submitted in 2014 were not addressed until 2016. A footnote says those grievances "involved claims by affected business owners that the provided compensation did not fully cover losses incurred as a result of the Project". An independent consultant was appointed in the summer of 2014 to help settle them and to check whether compensation had been paid in line with Bank policy; the report says the assessment helped address the complaints and "confirmed compliance". Separately, the report records that for an extended period environmental supervision and reporting were poor, "creating substantial risks for the livelihood of affected communities, health of workers": construction companies operated without adequate arrangements for waste disposal, and there were "obvious deficiencies in protecting workers' health and safety as well as in managing disturbance of communities residing in and around work sites". The completion report says the project was compliant with the resettlement policy, that all complaints were addressed, and that the Dartlo plan was completed without grievances or complaints.
dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 165 for this project. No document records a permanent relocation. The counts in the documents are of plan coverage for temporary moves and business interruption: 91 households and 84 businesses at Telavi, 44 residential buildings at Dartlo, 33 people at Kvareli.
dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents. The completion report records deficiencies in protecting workers' health and safety but no injury count.
dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.outcome: The works are finished and the project closed at the end of 2017. By the July 2016 plan update, two of the Dartlo owners due compensation for 2012 had still not been paid, four years after the works on their houses. The Telavi grievances were settled in 2016 and the lender's assessment found compensation had complied with its policy. No independent account of the Dartlo or Telavi compensation was found.

dartlo-telavi-rehabilitation-compensatio.confidence_note: The late payments at Dartlo and the two-year delay in answering the Telavi grievances are stated in the lender's own documents, one of them the borrower's plan update. Searches in Georgian for press or official accounts of the Telavi business compensation found nothing. The lender's conclusion cuts the other way on both counts: it says the project complied with the resettlement policy, that all complaints were addressed, and that Dartlo was completed without grievances. The numbers are small and the moves were temporary.

moinak-transmission-line-land-taken-befo.title: A power line built across farm land before the land acquisition plan was approved
moinak-transmission-line-land-taken-befo.place: Enbekshikazakh and four other districts, Almaty region, Kazakhstan
moinak-transmission-line-land-taken-befo.point: Esik, the centre of Enbekshikazakh district, as OpenStreetMap records it. Enbekshikazakh holds 222 of the 316 affected land users; the 220 kV line runs through this and four other districts of Almaty region.

lenders.name: World Bank (IBRD)
lenders.role: Kazakhstan Moinak Electricity Transmission Project, P114766, loan IBRD-77380. Approved 15 September 2009. US$48 million committed, US$44.73 million disbursed. The completion report of 30 October 2013 rates the outcome Satisfactory, as does the Independent Evaluation Group's review of 27 June 2014. The completion report says the Bank "was not able to ensure timely preparation by the Borrower and approval of LAP" and that construction of the line started without an approved plan.

companies.name: Kazakhstan Electricity Grid Operating Company (KEGOC)
companies.role: Formed as a state-owned entity in 1997, it operates Kazakhstan's 220, 500 and 1,150 kV transmission network and the national dispatch control. It built and now operates the 220 kV line and the Saryozek substation, and paid for the land acquisition and the compensation from its own funds.

moinak-transmission-line-land-taken-befo.community: The 220 kV line from the Moinak hydropower plant runs across farm and grazing land in Almaty region. The completion report of 30 October 2013 says KEGOC "acquired about 14 hectares of land for permanent use and 555 hectares for temporary use", all of it rural agricultural or grazing land, and that "in total, 316 persons (land users) have been affected. None had to be resettled, and all received reasonable cash compensation." The project's Land Acquisition Plan breaks the 316 down by district: 222 in Enbekshikazakh, 58 in Ili, 20 in Raimbek, 13 in Talgar and 3 in Kapshagai town, of whom 170 held the land in permanent or private ownership and 146 were leaseholders. It says 40 of them grew vegetables, 4 grew crops, 6 grew soy and the rest grew hay and lucerne, and that the harvest inside the line's right of way would be limited during construction. The order of events is the finding. A Land Acquisition Policy Framework was prepared before the project, but the specific plan that was supposed to set each land user's entitlement came later: the completion report says "construction of the line started prior to the Bank's formal approval of a Land Acquisition Plan", that the Bank's team alerted the client, and that a plan was then approved with "relevant retroactive measures" to bring the compensation into line with the Bank's resettlement policy. The plan itself, which carries no date on its cover page, records compensation payment agreements as still being concluded in May 2012. The completion report says all compensation was completed before the loan closed, and the Bank's reasoning for letting the works run on was that "the delay with the line construction would have been inadmissible". Its stated lesson is that even projects with limited land acquisition and no relocation of persons need the plan done on time.
moinak-transmission-line-land-taken-befo.displaced_note: ICIJ gives 316 for this project. That is the number the completion report gives for persons, specifically land users, affected. The same sentence says "none had to be resettled". No project document records anyone being relocated.
moinak-transmission-line-land-taken-befo.killed_note: No death is recorded in the project documents.
moinak-transmission-line-land-taken-befo.outcome: The line and the Saryozek substation are built and operating. The completion report says all 316 land users were paid before the loan closed, and both the report and the Independent Evaluation Group's review rate the project Satisfactory. Neither document says how long any land user waited, or how much any of them received.

moinak-transmission-line-land-taken-befo.confidence_note: The documented harm here is narrow. Nobody was relocated, the lender says everyone was paid, and no complaint, court case or news report about the land users was found in Russian or Kazakh searches. What is documented is that 14 hectares were taken permanently and 555 temporarily from 316 named categories of land user, and that the line was built before the plan that set their entitlements was approved, with compensation agreements still being concluded in May 2012. The amount paid to any land user is in an appendix the text refers to but does not reproduce.

osh-batken-isfana-road-no-land-taken.drop_reason: The outcome document records no land taken and nobody moved. The completion report of 27 June 2015, paragraph 2.4.7, states: "There was no land acquisition under either the parent project or AFs, and there were no project affected people (PAPs) under the parent project and AF1. The total compensation of about KGS 350,000 (US$7,000) was paid to seven project affected businesses under AF2." Those seven are road-side businesses at the Nookat pass, compensated for profit lost during construction; the borrower's own section of the same report confirms the government issued a decree in March 2013 to release the money and that the plan was translated into Kyrgyz and presented to the seven. Neither limb of the forward rule is met: no relocation count, and no harm left standing after payment. Checked in the outcome document: paragraphs 2.4.4 to 2.4.8 on social safeguards, the results framework, and the borrower's completion contribution. The brief's harm hits were context, not project harm. Its two 'count with a relocation verb' sentences were the June 2010 civil unrest in Osh and Jalal-Abad, in which about 400,000 people were displaced, which the report gives as a reason for implementation delay, and the resettlement framework's recital of the policy threshold of 200 displaced people. Its 'arrests, police or force' sentence was a dispute between the Ministry of Transport and the Ministry of Internal Affairs over who owned the road safety strategy, and its death sentences were road fatality rate indicators. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 32.

bishkek-osh-urban-infrastructure-nine-af.drop_reason: The outcome document counts nine affected people in total and records each of them paid. The completion report of 26 May 2016, paragraph 38, says four resettlement action plans were prepared, for Bash-Karasuu, Naryn, Isfana and Tash-Kumyr, that "there were nine project affected people", and that only one complaint was received, addressed at the first grievance stage. Its borrower annex itemises the payments: five farmers in Orok ayil aymak received KGS 240,000 between them; a Naryn resident received KGS 25,000 for the loss of a partially constructed house plus a land plot from the mayor's office; an Isfana farmer received KGS 28,820 and a land plot; two Tash-Kumyr residents were paid KGS 6,000 each for removed trees. Neither limb is met: nobody was relocated, and no compensation is recorded as unpaid or below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome document: the safeguards paragraphs, the grievance record and the borrower's social safeguards annex. The brief's 'compensation unpaid or late' hit was a June 2014 meeting with the Osh vice-mayor at which two Tash-Kumyr residents agreed a water main route through their orchards and were given an explanation about outstanding amounts; the relevant plan budgets 12,200 som for four years of apricot crop and saplings, and the completion report records the payment made. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 9.

armenia-electricity-supply-reliability-n.drop_reason: No outcome document counts land taken, households affected, or compensation left unpaid, and the harm language in the documents has delay to the works as its stated consequence. The completion report of 30 July 2024 says the utility's financial constraints "contributed to the documented delays, including those related to land acquisition and RAP compensations", and the next sentences give the consequence: the transmission rehabilitation finished in 2020, four years after the original closing date. Its social safeguards section says compliance was rated Satisfactory at closing, that all compliance reports found the abbreviated resettlement plans complied with the framework and national law, and that "most of the affected households (on average from 80 to 95 percent) were satisfied" with valuation, the size of compensation and the payment process. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 15 January 2025 repeats the 80 to 95 per cent. Neither limb is met. Checked in the outcome document: the social safeguards section, the factors affecting implementation, and the grievance record, which gives a garbled count of 157 grievances received and addressed. The resettlement policy framework of July 2015 says only that "it is expected that the number of persons to be relocated is minimal", a plan sentence with no outcome behind it. The brief's four harm hits were all recitals in the framework: the rule allowing possession before payment where compensation is pledged in court, the definition of replacement cost, the court deposit procedure, and the audit clause about livelihood restoration. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 440.

kakheti-regional-roads-31-plots-paid.drop_reason: Two outcome documents agree that the land taken was smaller than planned and that every owner was paid without complaint. The Independent Evaluation Group's field-based Project Performance Assessment Report of 17 June 2020 says the road department "completed the land acquisition for the section between Vaziani and Gombori in 2010 and for the section between Gombori and Telavi in 2012", that design changes meant "the land acquisition involved 31 land plots instead of the 174 expected at appraisal", and that the department "fully compensated all landowners in accordance with the provisions of the resettlement action plan and received no complaints". The review of 10 June 2016 gives the same 31 against 174 and the same conclusion. Neither limb is met: no relocation, and no compensation recorded as unpaid or below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome documents: the social safeguards sections of both, and the assessment report's appendix B. A trap worth recording: the assessment report covers two projects, and the paragraph beginning "At appraisal, no land acquisition or resettlements were envisioned... Minor land acquisitions had to take place during project implementation" sits under the heading for the Secondary and Local Roads Project, P086277, not for this one. The brief's harm hits were road-safety fatality indicators and the entitlement matrix's recital of compensation at replacement cost. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 422.

kyrgyz-second-rural-water-118-paid.drop_reason: The outcome document counts 118 affected people, mostly temporary, and records all of them paid. The completion report of 27 April 2015, paragraph 46, says the resettlement policy was triggered during implementation, that "118 Project Affected Persons (PAPs) in ten villages were identified", that they were "mainly affected by temporary restrictions to access or loss of trees and crops", and that "all PAPs were fully paid by the project closing date", with compensation of KGS 1,979,254, about US$50,000, paid exceptionally out of the credit itself. Neither limb is met. Checked in the outcome document: the safeguards section, the borrower's resettlement annex listing the ten villages, and the sections on the suspended sub-projects. One finding for another round rather than this row: the same report records that water schemes failed in 26 villages, and works were suspended before completion in Korumdu, Temir and Chelpek, under the predecessor Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Project, not under this one, "mostly associated with poor design of the water sources under the RWSSP", and that this project had to go back and fix them, deferring US$1.5 million of service work at Chelpek. The brief's harm hits were all framework recitals on eligibility and replacement cost. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 245.

albania-water-sector-resettlement-avoide.drop_reason: The outcome document says the project avoided resettlement and gives no count of land taken or compensation unpaid. The completion report of 25 September 2020, paragraph 56, says the late appointment of the social safeguards specialist "caused delays in implementing the social safeguard instruments (for example, the RAP), which resulted in changing the locations of one of the wells as the implementation of the RAP was stalled", and that "the project avoided resettlement by changing the routes of some of the water and wastewater lines in some areas". The one specific complaint it records is about a contractor that delayed restoring a local road to its original condition after finishing works, raised directly to the Bank through a social network account; no people are identified and no count is given. The Independent Evaluation Group's review of 25 June 2021 repeats the stalled plan and the avoided resettlement. Neither limb is met. Checked in the outcome document: paragraphs 55 and 56 on safeguards and the grievance record. The resettlement plan of January 2013 is plan-level only: 28 land owners along the new pipeline across four communes, with compensation estimated at 4,246,330 lek, about US$40,442, and a statement that no owner would be fully expropriated. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 137.

talimarjan-transmission-land-compensatio.drop_reason: The outcome document records land taken from leasehold farms with compensation completed and no complaints. The completion report of 22 December 2016, paragraphs 50 to 52, says the project needed about 12.03 ha permanently and 159.42 ha temporarily from 114 leasehold farms in Kashkadarya and Samarkand, 90 in the first and 24 in the second; that "in total 141 farmers and Hokimiyats in eight districts... received compensation"; that land acquisition and compensation payments were "completed by April 2013"; that apart from 26.7 ha for the substation the takes averaged 1.1 ha; and that "to date, no complaints have been recorded". It explains the shifting counts, 114 in the plan, 147 in a supervision aide memoire, 141 in the final list, by a government farm-consolidation programme and by an audit that found six farmers had been paid in error and asked them to return the money, and says the entitlement matrix was never modified. Neither limb is met: nobody was relocated and no compensation is recorded as unpaid or below replacement cost. Checked in the outcome document: the involuntary resettlement paragraphs, the borrower's section, which says "land compensations have been paid during 2010-2013", and the social impact discussion. The brief's harm hits were monitoring-indicator headings in the resettlement plan of September 2010 that list "number of people not receiving compensation in time" as a thing to be measured, and a risk-matrix row in the appraisal document naming non-compliance as a risk to be managed. ICIJ's estimate for this project is 114.
